planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in humus-rich soil that stays consistently moist to occasionally wet; naturalized across the Gulf South in ditches, pond margins, and low woodland edges, it tolerates ordinary garden conditions better than the true native swamp lily it resembles.

directions: Crinum erubescens is often sold and grown as an easier-care stand-in for the true Southern native Crinum americanum, forming similar clumps of strap-shaped leaves but tolerating merely moist garden beds rather than standing water. Umbels of two to six slender, white, trumpet-shaped flowers blushed with pink open atop a distinctive wine-red flowering stem from early summer into fall, each bloom carrying a light evening fragrance. Because the two species are frequently mislabeled in the nursery trade, gardeners should expect some variation in flower color and stem coloration even among plants sold under the same tag. Give it rich, humus-heavy soil that stays consistently damp and it will bulk up into a dependable, low-maintenance clump within a couple of seasons.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in rich, well-drained to moist soil in full sun for the strongest leaf color, moving container-grown plants to shelter well before the first frost in marginal zones.

directions: Giant Spider Lily is a robust tropical hybrid crinum, generally treated as a cross between Crinum asiaticum and Crinum zeylanicum, grown chiefly for its massive rosette of broad, arching, deep-green to purple-tinged leaves that can reach shoulder height on a mature clump. Tall, thick scapes push up through the foliage bearing dense umbels of fragrant, reddish-pink to deep rose flowers with narrow, spidery segments, blooming intermittently through the warm months. It needs consistent warmth and resents hard frost, so gardeners outside the deep tropics typically grow it as a large container specimen or tuck it into the warmest microclimate of the landscape. Full sun brings out the strongest leaf pigmentation, while a partly shaded site keeps the foliage a plainer green but the plant equally vigorous.

common_name: Stars and Stripes Crinum (Red-Striped Hybrid Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; a 1977 Thad Howard hybrid selected for its bold red-striped flowers.

directions: Stars and Stripes is a Thad Howard hybrid crinum pairing an African milk-and-wine parent with the Gulf Coast native Crinum erubescens, chosen for the exceptionally bold, dark red pinstripe running down the center of each glistening white petal. A single scape can carry eight to ten large, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers, and established clumps often send up a second flush of bloom in fall after the main midsummer show. The narrow, pleated, glossy leaves stay tidy and never sprawl as widely as some crinum hybrids, making it a reasonable choice for a smaller border. Like most crinum hybrids it wants humus-rich soil that does not dry out for long and rewards being left undisturbed for years rather than divided on a schedule.

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Sangria's Crinum bulbispermum parentage gives it more cold hardiness than most purple-leaved crinum selections.

directions: Sangria was found as a chance seedling in a South Carolina garden and later spread through the trade for its dramatic, glossy, deep-purple strap leaves rather than for the rosy-pink flowers alone. Because one parent traces back to the cold-hardy Crinum bulbispermum, Sangria tolerates winters that would damage many purple-leaved crinum selections, dying back to the bulb in hard freezes and returning reliably each spring. Clusters of trumpet-shaped pink flowers rise well above the foliage on tall scapes in late spring, with a second, often lighter bloom flush common in fall. Give it full sun for the darkest leaf color, since plants grown in shade tend to green up and lose much of the purple contrast that makes this cultivar distinctive.

planting.note: Plant rhizomatous bulbs 4-6 inches deep in humus-rich soil that stays consistently moist to occasionally flooded, in partial shade to full sun, mimicking the streambank and swamp-forest edges where it grows wild across the Florida Panhandle, Alabama, Mississippi, Georgia, and Louisiana.

directions: Choctaw spiderlily grows wild along streambanks and in swamp forests across the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana, and was only formally distinguished from the similar Hymenocallis caroliniana and H. occidentalis in the 1960s. Distinctive triangular floral bracts and a rhizomatous, spreading bulb habit separate it from those look-alike species in the field, though home gardeners will notice mainly the same fragrant white spider-form flowers with a central cup and long, narrow, curving tepals. It flowers in late spring into summer above strap-shaped leaves, doing best in soil that stays consistently moist to occasionally flooded, mirroring the streambank conditions where it naturally occurs. Because it is considered vulnerable in parts of its native range, gardeners should source bulbs only from reputable native-plant nurseries rather than wild-collected stock.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated bulbs 4-6 inches deep in humus-rich soil at the damp margin of a pond, rain garden, or low spot, in partial shade; native to cypress depression wetlands within pine flatwoods of the Florida Panhandle.

directions: Henry's spiderlily is a rare Florida Panhandle endemic known from only a handful of counties, where it grows at the damp edges of cypress depression wetlands within pine flatwoods. It is distinguished from its more common Hymenocallis relatives by pale green rather than pure white tepals paired with a white funnel-shaped corona, giving the flower a subtly two-toned look. Deciduous, narrow, bluish-green leaves die back in winter and re-emerge with the flowering scapes in the growing season, unlike the evergreen habit of some coastal spider lilies. Because wild populations are naturally limited, it suits collectors and native-plant enthusiasts growing nursery-propagated bulbs in consistently moist, humus-rich soil rather than serving as an everyday landscape plant.
sources: Florida Plant Atlas (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated bulbs with the neck at soil level in moist, well-drained sandy soil in full sun to light shade, replicating the seasonally moist pine flatwoods near Punta Gorda, Florida where the species survives in the wild.

directions: Punta Gorda spiderlily is a critically imperiled Florida endemic known only from the vicinity of Punta Gorda on the state's southern Gulf Coast, where it grows in seasonally moist pine flatwoods and along disturbed roadside edges. It closely resembles the widespread Hymenocallis latifolia but can be told apart by its narrower, firmer leaves and a staminal corona with more deeply cut, lacerate margins. Fragrant white spider-form flowers appear in mid- to late summer above the strap-shaped foliage, following the same general bloom pattern as its more common coastal relatives. Given its precarious wild status, it should only be grown from nursery-propagated bulbs, in evenly moist, well-drained soil with full sun to light shade similar to its native flatwoods habitat.
sources: Florida Plant Atlas (University of South Florida)
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Set bulbs 2-3 inches deep in spring in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; a deep watering after a dry spell reliably triggers a fresh flush of bloom.

directions: Zephyranthes robusta, native to Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay and long naturalized in Florida gardens, produces broader, showier lavender-pink trumpet flowers than most of the smaller rain lily species, each held singly atop a slender scape. Narrow, grayish-green, grass-like foliage stays low and tidy, making it a good edging or container plant that flowers repeatedly through summer and fall rather than in a single flush. Like other rain lilies it flushes into bloom within days of a good soaking rain after a dry spell, so plantings in average garden soil with occasional deep watering will flower more reliably than those kept constantly damp. It multiplies steadily by bulb offsets and is best left undisturbed for several years to build into a full, floriferous clump.
